data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Your body contains tens of trillions of cells with different jobs. This lesson compares typical animal and photosynthetic plant cells using a factory analogy.

1. Read **The Factory You Are Made Of**. Each part has a JOB — that is the whole idea.
2. Learn the parts in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Study the **Job Chart** — it pairs each part with what it actually does.
4. Sort the cards in **Plant, Animal, or Both?** Use the pictured typical cells; not every plant or animal cell has every illustrated feature.
5. Take the quiz. It asks WHY, not just WHAT.
6. Fill in the **Cornell Notes** page in your own words — that page is your study sheet later.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Factory Floor** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: Build a Cell That Could Live Somewhere Else** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.
9. Read the **The Factory Floor Plan** map by department before you take notes — structure fits function every time.

If you finish everything, you will be able to explain a cell without a diagram in front of you. That is the real goal. 🔬

Picture panels: Cell discoveries and plant structure; Animal cells and boundaries; Energy-processing organelles; Water and support. Text-free illustrations use editable captions and image-specific descriptions. Diagrams simplify scale, anatomy and processes; colors and tokens are explained in captions. Follow the lesson text for scientific context. Educator review is pending.

history.title: The Factory You Are Made Of
history.data:
## The Factory You Are Made Of

A microscope can turn a tiny patch of tissue into a landscape. Robert Hooke described boxlike compartments in cork in 1665 and called them cells. He saw walls left by dead plant cells, not all the working parts of a living cell.

Cells are the basic units of living organisms. Adult human bodies contain tens of trillions, with the number depending on the person. This lesson compares typical animal cells and photosynthetic plant cells. Bacteria have a different organization, and specialized cells do not all contain the same parts.

Think of a cell as a factory, but remember that the parts do not think or make plans. The **cell membrane** is a selective boundary: its lipids and proteins affect what crosses. Movement depends on molecular properties, concentration differences and transport proteins; some transport requires energy.

The **nucleus** contains most of a typical plant or animal cell's DNA. Cells use different combinations of genes, including many shared ones. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA. Some specialized cells, such as mature human red blood cells, lack a nucleus.

**Mitochondria** carry out major stages of aerobic cellular respiration. Energy from food molecules is transferred into ATP, which powers cellular work. Energy is transformed, not created. Plant cells also have mitochondria. Some steps of breaking down glucose occur in the cytosol outside mitochondria.

The **cytoplasm** includes the cytosol, a watery gel, and structures outside the nucleus. **Ribosomes** join amino acids to make proteins. Many proteins destined for secretion or membranes are made at the rough **endoplasmic reticulum**, where processing begins. Smooth ER has other roles, including lipid production. Transport vesicles carry materials to the **Golgi apparatus**, which modifies and sorts many proteins for delivery. Not every protein follows this route.

A typical photosynthetic plant cell has a **cell wall** outside its membrane, **chloroplasts**, and a large central **vacuole**. The wall provides support; chloroplasts use light energy in photosynthesis; the vacuole stores water and other materials. Many plant cells, including onion bulb cells, lack chloroplasts. Animals lack cell walls and chloroplasts, but both groups have membrane-bound transport compartments.

Water entering plant cells can build **turgor pressure**, pressing the cell contents against the wall. Water loss can reduce this pressure and make leaves droop. Vacuoles need not empty completely, and wilting can have other causes.

Use the pictures to connect structures with functions. Compare an onion cell with a green leaf cell: what is shared, what differs, and what evidence would a microscope actually let you see?

questions.question: A muscle cell contains far more mitochondria than a skin cell. Why?
options: Muscle cells are larger so they need more of every part
Mitochondria help muscles hold their shape
Skin cells cannot make mitochondria
Muscle cells need much more usable energy to contract
questions.correctAnswer: Muscle cells need much more usable energy to contract

questions.question: Do plant cells have mitochondria?
options: Yes — they need to release energy from sugar just like animal cells
No — chloroplasts replace them and make all the energy a plant needs
Only at night, when photosynthesis stops and the plant has to switch over
Only in the roots, where there is no sunlight for chloroplasts to use
questions.correctAnswer: Yes — they need to release energy from sugar just like animal cells

questions.question: A houseplant droops after a week without water. Which part best explains the drooping?
options: The cell walls dissolved without water, so the plant could not stand
Water loss reduced vacuole volume and turgor pressure
The chloroplasts stopped making food, so the plant ran out of energy
The nucleus shut down to save energy until water returned
questions.correctAnswer: Water loss reduced vacuole volume and turgor pressure

questions.question: Why is the cell membrane described as 'selectively permeable'?
options: It only opens at certain times of day
It can be seen only with a microscope
It lets some substances through while blocking others
It permits everything in but nothing out
questions.correctAnswer: It lets some substances through while blocking others

questions.question: Robert Hooke looked at cork and saw empty boxes. What was he actually seeing?
options: The cell walls left behind by dead plant cells
Living animal cells swimming in fluid
Bacteria growing on the cork
Air bubbles trapped in the wood
questions.correctAnswer: The cell walls left behind by dead plant cells

questions.question: Pick any TWO cell parts and explain how each one's structure fits its job.
questions.expectedAnswer: Membrane lipids form a selective barrier and transport proteins help particular substances cross. Mitochondrial inner-membrane folds provide area for proteins involved in ATP production. Shapes help functions but model colors and sizes are conventions.

questions.question: Your friend says 'plants don't need mitochondria because they make their own food.' Explain the flaw in that reasoning.
questions.expectedAnswer: Photosynthesis makes sugars using light energy; cellular respiration transfers food energy into ATP. Plant cells use mitochondria in major stages of aerobic respiration, just as animal cells do.

reflections.text: Which cell part would you least want to lose, and why? Defend your choice.
The reading says 'structure fits function.' Name something outside biology where that is also true.

data.question: If I have 30 trillion cells, how do they all know what to do? 🤯
data.answer: Most human cells contain similar nuclear DNA but use different combinations of genes, including many shared genes. Specialized cells differ; mature human red blood cells have no nucleus. The total cell count varies between people.

data.question: Are viruses cells?
data.answer: Viruses are not cells. They contain genetic material inside a protein coat; some also have a lipid envelope. They depend on host cells to reproduce.

data.question: Why is celery crunchy but a hamburger is not? 🥬
data.answer: Plant cell walls and turgor help make fresh celery crisp. Food texture also depends on tissues, preparation and water content; it is not a complete cell-type test.

data.question: Can a single cell be large enough to see?
data.answer: Cells differ greatly in size and shape. A bird egg contains a large egg cell, but its shell and egg white are not parts of that single cell. Long nerve cells and large egg cells illustrate different kinds of size.

data.question: Do my cells ever get replaced?
data.answer: Replacement rates differ by tissue. Many lining and blood cells are replaced regularly, while some nerve cells can persist for decades. A whole body does not replace all its cells on one schedule.

data.question: Is it true mitochondria used to be bacteria? 🦠
data.answer: That is the leading scientific explanation, called endosymbiotic theory: an ancient cell engulfed a bacterium and they became partners. Mitochondria still have their own separate DNA, which is strong evidence for it.

data.title: Build a Cell That Could Live Somewhere Else
data.instructions: Design a hypothetical eukaryotic cell model for one environment. Explain structure and function, identify tradeoffs, and mark guesses. A design proposal is not evidence that cells evolve parts because they need them.
data.fitReason: The reading ends on 'structure fits function.' A design task that changes an environment forces students to reason from an organelle's job to its shape and number, instead of labeling a diagram.

brief.context: A museum wants hypothetical eukaryotic cell models for a shaded pond, a sunlit pond or moving freshwater. Use real cell parts and identify what your model cannot establish about survival.
brief.audience: Museum visitors aged 10 and up, and the museum educator who checks the science
brief.drivingQuestion: For one environment, which cell parts would you make bigger, smaller, more numerous, or shaped differently, and how does each change follow from that part's job?
brief.seedDirection: Start from the job each organelle already does in the lesson. Then ask what that job needs more or less of in your environment.
lockedLessonFacts: The cell membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and blocks others.
A typical eukaryotic nucleus contains most cellular DNA.
Mitochondria transfer food energy into ATP; abundance varies with cell type and demands.
A typical photosynthetic plant cell has a wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole; not all plant cells have chloroplasts.
Structure fits function: a part's shape and number match its job.
openQuestions: Does this environment have light? If not, what happens to chloroplasts?
Is water scarce or everywhere, and what does that mean for the vacuole?
Does the cell need to hold its shape against pressure or flow?
Where would energy come from if there is no sunlight?
stakeholders: Museum visitors who will read the card
The educator checking that every claim is grounded
Classmates building cells for other environments
The exhibit builders who need a clear drawing
criteria: Uses at least five real organelles from the lesson, each with its real job
Every change in size, number, or shape has a one-sentence structure-fits-function reason
State what evidence would be needed to test each predicted advantage; more of an organelle is not automatically better.
The card uses at least four glossary words correctly
constraints: Only changes in size, number, or shape; no new organelles
Model fits on one sheet or one shoebox
brief.deliverable: A labeled model or drawing of the adapted cell, plus a museum card that names the environment, lists each changed part, and gives the structure-fits-function reason for every change.

parallelExample.context: A student compared a heart muscle cell with a skin cell.
parallelExample.move: Instead of listing parts, she asked what each cell's job needed. The heart cell contracts nonstop, so she predicted far more mitochondria; the skin cell protects and is replaced often, so she predicted fewer. The real cells matched her reasoning.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It is the same move you are making, in reverse: she reasoned from the job to the number of parts. You will reason from the environment to the job, then to the parts.

supports.frameStarter: In ____, a cell needs to ____. So I would make the ____ ____, because its job is ____.
frameChoices: Change the number of mitochondria based on how much energy the environment demands
Change the vacuole based on how much water is available
Change the membrane or add a wall based on pressure or flow
Remove or keep chloroplasts based on whether light reaches the cell
coachPrompts: Which of your changes would a visitor question first, and what lesson fact answers them?
Did you change a part because it looks cool or because its job demands it?
What does your cell do for energy if there is no light?

data.coachHint: Every arrow on your drawing should be able to finish the sentence 'because its job is…'. If it cannot, the change is decoration.
